title: "peace be with you"
hook: "peace be with you" — the handshake in the middle
tomorrow: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mass, scene one: the readings, and the whole room standing for the Gospel. Your line was: the story enters the room. Who did you really listen to? Day four.

Here's the moment first-time visitors remember. The Mass is quiet and formal. Candles, a priest at the altar, everyone facing forward, nobody talking. And then, out of nowhere, everyone turns around. The person behind you sticks out a hand. The teenager next to you, who hasn't looked up from the floor, says peace be with you. A couple kisses. A little kid waves at the whole row. For about thirty seconds, a room full of people who mostly don't know each other shakes hands. Then everyone turns back to the front as if nothing happened. Today, scene two of the Mass, and the handshake in the middle of it.
screen: `EVERYONE FACING FORWARD.` → `THEN EVERYONE TURNS AROUND.` → `THE HANDSHAKE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: After the story comes the table. Catholics call the second half of the Mass the Liturgy of the Eucharist. Bread and wine are carried up to the altar, the priest prays over them, and the whole room says the Our Father together. Then, just before people come forward to receive communion, the sign of peace. Where does it come from? Start with Easter night. In John's Gospel, the frightened friends of Jesus are hiding behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. His first words, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Peace be to you." Not a scolding for running away. Peace. In the Greek, eirene, and behind it the Hebrew greeting shalom, which means more than quiet. It means whole, complete, nothing missing. The first Christians greeted each other with more than a handshake. Paul's letters tell them to greet one another with a holy kiss, and for centuries worship included what was called the kiss of peace. There's a reason it sits right before communion in the Catholic Mass. Jesus once said that if you're bringing a gift to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, leave the gift there, go and make peace first, then come back. So before people go up to the table, they turn to whoever's beside them. Not their best friend. Whoever happens to be there. It's short on purpose. It isn't a chat. It's a sign: before we go any further, we're at peace with each other. Some older Catholic rites put the gesture earlier in the Mass, and the words and the gesture vary from country to country: a bow, a nod, a handshake. The meaning holds: turn to the stranger.
screen: `AFTER THE STORY, THE TABLE.` · `PEACE BE TO YOU — EASTER NIGHT.` · `SHALOM — WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `MAKE PEACE, THEN COME TO THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of three people. On the first breath, someone you love. On the second, someone you barely know: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who sold you coffee. On the third, someone you're not at peace with right now. With each breath out, picture turning to them and offering your hand. If you pray, you can wish each of them peace.
The Mass, scene two. The table, and just before it, the sign of peace: turning to whoever is beside you. Fourth word.
Your line: turn to the stranger. Today, give one person you don't know a real greeting: a look in the eye, a hello, a small kindness. Day four.

screen: `DAY 4 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BREAD, WINE, "DO THIS IN MEMORY OF ME."`

howItsDone: At Mass, after the Our Father and before communion, the priest invites the people to offer each other a sign of peace, and people turn to those nearby with a handshake, a bow or a nod, saying "peace be with you."

fork.setup: you're one of Jesus's friends, hiding behind a locked door on Easter night after running away. he's suddenly standing in the room. what's the first thing he says?
fork.reveal: "peace be to you." not a scolding. the greeting Catholics pass to each other at Mass starts here.

original.note: Greek: peace. the word John's Gospel puts in the risen Jesus's mouth, carrying the Hebrew shalom behind it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a friendly pause so people can say hi.
what it means: a sign of being at peace with each other before going to the table.
what a scholar hears: the ancient kiss of peace; the Roman Mass places it before communion, while some other rites have it earlier, echoing Matthew 5:23–24.
